topic: Pilot run without pre-agreed success criteria
stem: A health insurer ran a ten-week pilot of a Claude-based claims-triage assistant with twelve adjusters. At the readout the executive sponsor calls it a clear success: adjusters liked it, weekly usage grew, and no bad outcome was escalated. There is no written definition of success from before the pilot, and the adjusters' own pre-pilot triage accuracy was never measured. The sponsor wants to fund rollout to four hundred adjusters. What is the most defensible position to take?

options.text: Treat the pilot as producing no decision-grade evidence: agree now what result would have counted as failure, measure the adjusters' current baseline, and re-run against it.

Approve the rollout. Ten weeks of voluntary usage growth and positive adjuster sentiment are the leading indicators that matter for an assistive tool, and triage accuracy is hard to measure reliably at twelve-adjuster scale.

Approve the rollout and instrument an accuracy dashboard in production, where four hundred adjusters will generate a far larger sample than the pilot could and any quality problem will surface quickly.
Extend the pilot by a further ten weeks with more adjusters so the satisfaction and usage trends are confirmed on a bigger group before rollout budget is committed.

explanation.correct: A pilot with no criterion written down before it starts cannot fail, and a test that cannot fail carries no information. Every observation the sponsor cites — sentiment, usage growth, absence of escalations — is compatible with a triage assistant that is worse than the adjusters it assists, because nobody measured the adjusters. The only way out is to state the decision metric and the baseline that make the claim falsifiable, then collect that measurement. Doing so costs weeks; scaling on an unfalsifiable result costs the rollout.

distractors.B: Usage and sentiment are adoption signals, not quality signals, and they are exactly the signals a fluent-but-wrong assistant produces. Sentiment is worth tracking after you have a quality measure, never instead of one.
distractors.C: This defers measurement until after the irreversible commitment. A larger sample does help precision, but only if you have already agreed what number decides the question and what the comparison point is — neither exists here.
distractors.D: Repeating a design that cannot produce evidence produces more of no evidence. The defect is the absent criterion and baseline, not the sample size or the duration. Adding participants improves the precision of a measurement nobody is taking.

explanation.concept: A pilot is an experiment, and an experiment needs a pre-registered outcome that could come out against you. Before a pilot begins, write down the metric, the threshold, the baseline it is compared against, and who decides. Without those four, the pilot will be narrated as a success whatever happens, and it cannot support a production decision.
explanation.tip: When a stem tells you no success criteria existed and no baseline was taken, no option that approves or defers is defensible. The answer is always to restore falsifiability, even when the stem makes that sound like delay.

topic: Why criterion-free pilots produce no evidence
stem: Why is an AI pilot that finished without success criteria agreed in advance treated as worthless evidence for a production go/no-go decision?

options.text: Pilots run on non-representative traffic almost by construction, so their measurements rarely generalise to production volumes or to the full diversity of real inputs.
Any outcome can be narrated as a success afterwards, so the pilot could not have disconfirmed the hypothesis it was meant to test.
Return on investment cannot be computed without a documented per-request cost, which pilots rarely capture.
Evaluation harnesses cannot be constructed retrospectively once the pilot traffic has already been served.

explanation.correct: The value of a pilot comes entirely from its capacity to produce a negative result. When the threshold is set after the data is seen, the threshold moves to wherever the data landed, and the exercise degrades into a demonstration. Demonstrations tell you the system can work once; they say nothing about whether it works at the rate the business needs. This is why pre-registration of the metric and threshold is the single most valuable thing an architect can insist on before a pilot begins.

distractors.A: Pilot traffic is often unrepresentative, and that is a real threat to validity, but it is a separate problem that a well-designed pilot mitigates through sampling. It is not why a criterion-free pilot is uninformative.
distractors.C: Cost per request is one possible success criterion among many. The defect is the absence of any pre-agreed criterion, not the absence of this particular one. Plenty of pilots are decided on quality alone and are perfectly sound experiments.
distractors.D: Harnesses and graders can be built after the fact and replayed over logged pilot traffic. The irrecoverable loss is the commitment to a threshold, not the tooling. You can rebuild the harness later; you cannot rebuild a pre-commitment after seeing the data.

explanation.concept: Treat a pilot as a pre-registered experiment: metric, threshold, baseline, decision owner, all fixed before traffic flows. A result that could not have come out against the proposal is not a result. This applies with extra force to AI systems, where fluent output makes informal impressions systematically optimistic.
explanation.tip: The word to look for in these stems is falsifiable. If nothing the pilot could have produced would have stopped the project, the pilot was theatre regardless of how well it went.

topic: Parallel run before cutover on a safety-critical classifier
stem: A national grid operator is replacing a fifteen-year-old rules engine that assigns a hazard category to field work orders. A misclassification that downgrades a hazard sends a crew out without gas-detection equipment, which the safety team logs as a reportable incident. Offline evaluation on 4,000 historical work orders shows the Claude-based classifier agrees with the rules engine on 96% of them; on the 160 disagreements, a safety expert judged the classifier correct in 71 cases. Vendor support for the rules engine ends in eight weeks, and the safety team will not make the classifier authoritative without evidence it does not downgrade hazards on live work. Which rollout approach fits?

options.text: Cut over on the support deadline and keep the rules engine deployed as a fallback that operations can re-enable within one shift if reportable incidents rise above the current baseline.
Restrict the classifier to the lowest hazard category first and expand one category at a time, limiting the blast radius of any single misclassification during the early weeks.

Run both systems on live work orders with the rules engine still authoritative, route every disagreement to a safety reviewer, and cut over once the disagreement log shows the classifier is not the side downgrading hazards.
Expand the offline evaluation to 20,000 historical work orders and gate cutover on reaching 99% agreement with the rules engine, giving a much tighter confidence interval than 4,000 cases.

explanation.correct: The safety team has asked for a specific piece of evidence — that the classifier does not downgrade hazards on live work — and a parallel run is the only design that produces it without exposing crews. Keeping the legacy engine authoritative means no live decision depends on the new classifier while the disagreement stream is adjudicated. The disagreement rate is already known to be about 4%, so the reviewer load is bounded and the eight-week window is realistic. The adjudicated log is the artefact the safety team signs against.

distractors.A: A fallback re-enabled within one shift still means real crews were dispatched on the classifier's decisions during that shift. Where the failure is a reportable safety incident rather than a degraded experience, detecting harm after it occurs is not risk control.
distractors.B: A hazard downgrade cannot occur in the lowest category because there is nothing beneath it. This design deliberately excludes the failure mode the safety team cares about, so it accumulates weeks of evidence about everything except the thing in question.
distractors.D: Agreement with the rules engine is not the target. The stem already shows the engine is wrong on 71 of 160 disagreements, so it is not ground truth; optimising toward it would reward the classifier for reproducing legacy errors.

explanation.concept: When you are replacing a system whose errors are expensive and the legacy system is not a trustworthy oracle, run both live with the incumbent authoritative and adjudicate the disagreements. The disagreement set is small, information-dense, and is the evidence a safety or risk owner can actually sign. Shadow the decision, do not gamble it.
explanation.tip: Two details do the work here: the incumbent is demonstrably wrong sometimes, which kills any agreement-rate gate, and the harm is a downgrade, which kills any staged rollout that starts at the bottom of the scale.

topic: Decoupling prompt releases from the application release train
stem: An online grocer ships a Claude-powered substitution suggester inside its picker mobile app. Prompts live in the application repository as string constants and ship with the binary; the mobile release train runs fortnightly and app-store review adds a further two to four days. A prompt change last month caused allergen-conflicting substitutions to be suggested, and the corrected prompt took nine days to reach pickers. The postmortem action item is titled "reduce time-to-remediate for prompt-caused defects". Which change addresses that action item most directly?

options.text: Add a regression evaluation suite to continuous integration that blocks the merge of any prompt change failing the allergen test cases before it can reach the release train.
Move to a weekly release train and pre-stage signed builds so app-store review overlaps with the internal QA window rather than following it.
Add a server-side output filter that drops any suggested substitution conflicting with allergens declared on the customer's account before it is shown to the picker.
Serve prompts from a versioned server-side configuration store the app fetches at session start, so a prompt version can be reverted without an app release.

explanation.correct: The action item names remediation time, and remediation time here is dominated by a structural coupling: prompt text is a compiled artefact, so reverting a prompt requires a binary release and a store review. Decoupling prompts into a versioned configuration surface the client fetches makes rollback a configuration change measured in minutes and makes the prompt independently versionable, which is also what lets you attribute a behaviour change to a specific prompt version later. Nothing else in the list moves the nine days.

distractors.A: A blocking eval suite is the right prevention control and should exist, but it reduces the probability of a bad prompt shipping rather than the time to pull one back. A defect that slips past the suite still takes nine days to fix.
distractors.B: Halving the release cadence roughly halves the worst case but leaves remediation measured in days and still hostage to store review. It also does nothing for prompt changes discovered hours after a release lands.
distractors.C: An allergen guardrail is a sound safety control for this specific harm and is worth adding, but it patches one class of bad output. The next prompt defect will be something else, and it will again take nine days.

explanation.concept: Prompts change far more often than application code and are the most common source of behaviour change, so they must be deployable and revertible on their own timeline. Treat a prompt as a versioned runtime artefact with its own release and rollback path, not as source code compiled into a client you cannot recall.
explanation.tip: Read what the postmortem action item actually says. Prevention options and remediation options both look responsible; only one of them answers a stem framed around time-to-remediate.

topic: Quality alerting for a run team inheriting an AI service
stem: A telco is transferring a Claude-based tier-one support deflection bot to a 24/7 network operations centre that has never operated an AI system. The NOC's entire alert catalogue is availability- and latency-based. The failure the product team fears is that the bot returns a fluent, confidently wrong answer while every endpoint is healthy and every latency objective is green. Which additions to the NOC's alert catalogue address that specific failure mode? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: An alert on p99 model-call latency, since degraded answer quality reliably shows up first as slower generation.
A rolling alert on the proportion of conversations that end in escalation to a human agent, compared against the same weekday in the previous week.
An alert on daily token spend deviating from the thirty-day trend by more than the agreed tolerance.
An alert on the rate at which answers fail the citation checker that grounds each claim in a knowledge-base article.
An alert on 5xx rates from the model gateway, paging the on-call engineer as soon as the error budget for the hour has been exhausted rather than at the end of the day.

explanation.correct: Escalation rate and groundedness-check failure rate are both quality proxies that move when the bot starts being wrong, and neither depends on anything being unavailable. Escalation rate is the cheapest end-to-end signal a NOC can act on: it is already collected, it is a user-revealed judgement that the answer was not good enough, and week-on-week comparison controls for the weekday pattern. The citation checker gives the leading signal, catching ungrounded answers before a customer has to give up on one.

distractors.A: The premise is false. An AI system's answers can degrade with latency completely unchanged, which is precisely the failure the stem describes; slow generation and wrong generation are independent. Latency alerting earns its place in the catalogue on its own merits, just not for this.
distractors.E: This is a well-formed availability alert and it belongs in the catalogue, but it is the kind of alert the NOC already has. It cannot fire during the described failure because nothing is erroring.
distractors.C: Spend anomalies are worth watching for runaway loops and abuse, and cost ownership does transfer with the system. It is a financial signal, not a quality one, and it will not move when answers become wrong.

explanation.concept: An AI system can fail while fully available. A run team inheriting one therefore needs quality signals — escalation, override, thumbs-down, groundedness, guardrail-trip rates — alongside the availability signals it already runs, plus a documented action for each. Handing an AI service to a team whose only alerts are uptime alerts hands them a system whose worst failure is invisible.
explanation.tip: Count the options that are both true and responsive before you answer. Cost and 5xx alerts are genuinely good practice, which is what makes them tempting; the stem asked only about the fluent-and-wrong failure mode.

topic: Runbook content for third-party L1 and L2 support
stem: A logistics company is handing a Claude-based customs-document extraction service to a managed-services vendor that will own L1 and L2 response under a 24/7 contract. The vendor's engineers have no context on the system and will act on the runbook alone at three in the morning. Which items belong in that runbook? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: The architecture decision record explaining why customs extraction was implemented as a fixed workflow rather than an autonomous agent, with the options rejected.
The exact procedure to revert to the previously pinned prompt and model versions, including the command, the flag, and whose approval is required.
A catalogue of failure signatures already seen in production, each with its observable symptom and the first diagnostic query to run against the trace store.
The full evaluation set and grading rubric used to gate releases, so the vendor can re-run evaluation overnight and approve a fix before it ships to production.
The escalation path with named owners and the explicit conditions that require waking the product team rather than the vendor continuing to work the incident.

explanation.correct: A runbook is judged by whether a stranger can act correctly from it under time pressure. Rollback procedure, known failure signatures with a first diagnostic step, and an escalation path with explicit wake-up conditions are all directly actionable at three in the morning and all remove a judgement call the vendor is not equipped to make. Naming who approves a rollback matters as much as the command itself, because an unapproved revert during an incident is its own incident.

distractors.A: Design rationale belongs in the handover pack and helps the vendor over months, but nobody debugs an incident by reading why the pattern was chosen. Putting background material into a runbook dilutes the pages people need at speed.
distractors.D: Release gating stays with whoever owns the change, and an L1/L2 vendor approving its own fixes against the release evals inverts the accountability the contract sets up. The evals belong in the handover pack and the CI pipeline, not the incident runbook.

explanation.concept: Write runbooks for the person on call, not for the person who built the system. Every entry should be a symptom, a diagnostic, an action, and a boundary condition for escalating. Anything that requires design context to apply is documentation, and belongs somewhere the on-call engineer is not reading at three in the morning.
explanation.tip: Test each candidate entry against a single question: can a tired stranger execute it without asking anyone? Explanatory artefacts always feel valuable, which is why they are the classic over-inclusion in this item type.

topic: Production readiness gap in degraded-mode procedure
stem: Two weeks before go-live for a Claude-based prior-authorisation summariser at a regional health plan, the production readiness review returns green on every item except one: there is no agreed procedure for what clinicians do when the summariser is unavailable or when a guardrail withholds its output. Volume is 3,000 authorisations a day and the fully manual path takes a nurse about twelve minutes per case. What is the next step?

options.text: Define and rehearse the degraded-mode procedure, including which cases queue and which are triaged manually, and hold go-live until clinical operations signs it off.
Go live on schedule and add the degraded-mode procedure to the first post-launch iteration, since every other readiness item is green and the expected outage rate is low.
Add an automatic fallback to a cheaper model tier so a summary is always produced, which removes the need for a manual procedure entirely.
Fund enough additional nursing capacity to absorb the six hundred nurse-hours a day that a total outage of the summariser would create.

explanation.correct: Three thousand cases at twelve minutes each is six hundred nurse-hours a day, so the manual path demonstrably cannot absorb full volume. That arithmetic is what turns a paperwork gap into a blocking finding: the degraded mode is not "do it by hand", it is a triage rule about which authorisations wait and which get human attention first, and that rule is a clinical decision the plan's operations leadership must own. A readiness review exists to surface exactly this before go-live, not to be overridden by it.

distractors.B: Deferring the one unresolved item to after launch is deferring it to the moment it is needed under pressure. The all-green context is the trap: readiness is a conjunction, and the outstanding item is the one that governs behaviour when things go wrong.
distractors.C: A guardrail withholding output is a deliberate safety action, so routing around it to a different model tier defeats the control rather than degrading gracefully. It also produces clinical summaries with no one having decided that the substitute is acceptable for this use.
distractors.D: Staffing for a total outage sizes the organisation to its worst hour permanently. Degraded modes are handled by prioritising and deferring work, not by holding six hundred hours of standby capacity for a low-probability event.

explanation.concept: Production readiness for an AI feature includes a rehearsed answer to "what do users do when this is not available or refuses". Where the manual fallback cannot absorb full volume — and for any feature that has genuinely displaced work, it cannot — the degraded mode is a prioritisation policy owned by the business, agreed and practised before launch.
explanation.tip: Do the arithmetic the stem hands you. Three thousand times twelve minutes is the whole item: it tells you the manual path is not a fallback, which converts the missing procedure from a formality into a launch blocker.

topic: Exit criteria between rings of a phased rollout
stem: In a ring-based phased rollout of a production AI feature, what should determine when the next ring opens?

options.text: A fixed calendar interval fixed in the release plan and communicated to stakeholders in advance.
Pre-declared exit criteria evaluated against the current ring's own production traffic.
Completion of user training and enablement for the population in the next ring.
The point at which support ticket volume from the current ring falls back to its pre-launch level.

explanation.correct: Rings exist to convert exposure into evidence. Each ring must therefore carry thresholds — quality, escalation rate, error budget, override rate — written down before it opens, so that the decision to widen is a measurement and not a mood. Fixing the criteria in advance also fixes the rollback trigger, since the same thresholds define when you shrink the ring rather than grow it. Without them a phased rollout is only a slower version of shipping everything at once.

distractors.A: Calendar gating gives the appearance of caution while guaranteeing the next ring opens whether or not the current one behaved. It is worth pairing a minimum soak time with criteria, but the interval alone decides nothing.
distractors.C: Enablement readiness is a genuine precondition for the next ring and can hold it closed, but it is a constraint on the receiving population rather than evidence about how the system is performing.
distractors.D: Ticket volume returning to baseline can mean the feature is healthy, or that users have quietly stopped using it. Silence is ambiguous, which makes it a poor sole gate. Pair it with an explicit usage measure before treating quiet as good news.

explanation.concept: Phased delivery is only risk control if each phase has pre-declared, measurable exit criteria and a matching rollback trigger. Set them before the ring opens, evaluate them on that ring's real traffic, and give someone the explicit authority to hold the gate closed.
explanation.tip: Whenever an option gates on time rather than on measurement, treat it as suspect. Phasing without criteria is theatre, and the exam tests that distinction repeatedly.

topic: Scoping customer notice for a model version retirement
stem: A legal-tech vendor sells a contract-clause extraction API to sixty law firms. Its service pins one Claude model version, and its customer contracts promise that extraction behaviour will not change without ninety days' notice. The pinned version has entered its deprecation window, with retirement eleven months away. Six customers run their own downstream regression suites keyed to exact output strings. What should the vendor do first?

options.text: Introduce a versioned API surface, keeping v1 on the current behaviour and offering v2 on the successor model, and let each firm migrate on its own schedule.

Send the ninety-day notice to all sixty firms immediately, since the contractual clock should start as early as possible and the underlying model is definitely changing at some point in the next eleven months.
Run the successor model in shadow against production traffic, diff the outputs per customer, and use the diff to determine who is materially affected and what the notice must actually say.
Insert an output-normalisation layer that rewrites the successor's output into the current model's formatting so that no customer observes a change at all.

explanation.correct: The contract is about behaviour change, and nobody yet knows what changes. Shadowing the successor over real traffic and diffing per customer converts an unknown into a scoped list: which firms see differences, on which clause types, and whether the differences are formatting or substance. That determines who must be notified, what the notice says, and which of the six string-keyed customers needs hands-on migration support. Eleven months is ample time to measure first; a notice sent before the diff exists will be wrong and will have to be re-sent.

distractors.A: A pinned model version cannot be kept alive past its retirement date, so v1 has a hard expiry the vendor does not control. Offering customers an indefinite migration schedule on a surface that will disappear creates a commitment the vendor cannot honour.
distractors.B: Blanket notice ninety days out on an eleven-month horizon burns the notice on speculation. Worse, it says nothing useful, because the vendor cannot yet describe what will change — and vague change notices generate exactly the support load the six string-keyed customers will create.
distractors.D: Normalising formatting hides only formatting. Extraction differences that are semantic will pass straight through the layer while the vendor has told itself nobody is affected, and the layer then becomes permanent coupling to a retired model's quirks.

explanation.concept: Model retirement is a migration project, and migrations start with measurement. Diff the successor against the incumbent on your own production traffic, segmented by customer or use case, before you write a notice or a plan. The diff tells you the blast radius; the notice, the timeline, and the support plan all derive from it.
explanation.tip: Note who controls the deadline. When retirement is set by someone outside your organisation, any option that promises customers an open-ended timeline is unimplementable no matter how customer-friendly it sounds.

topic: Sunsetting a legacy engine with unverified carve-out rules
stem: A manufacturer replaced a two-hundred-rule expert system for warranty-claim eligibility with a Claude-based decisioner six months ago. The old engine still runs in parallel at £14,000 a month in licence and hosting, and nobody has decommissioned it. Pressed by the finance director, the team's honest answer is that three of the two hundred rules encode a regulatory carve-out that nobody has verified in the new system. What is the correct sunset action?

options.text: Decommission now and add a post-hoc filter for the carve-out later if a claim is ever found to have been handled incorrectly under it.
Keep the old engine running permanently as the authoritative check on carve-out cases, treating the licence cost as the price of demonstrable compliance.
Port all two hundred rules verbatim into the decisioner's system prompt so behaviour is provably equivalent, then decommission the engine.
Write evaluations that exercise the three carve-out rules specifically, confirm the decisioner honours them, add those evaluations to the regression suite, and decommission on a dated plan.

explanation.correct: The blocker is precisely identified — three rules, unverified — so the work is small and targeted: build cases that exercise those rules, check the decisioner's behaviour, and put the cases in the regression suite so the carve-out cannot silently regress after the engine is gone. Adding them to the suite is what makes decommissioning safe rather than merely brave, because it replaces the old engine's role as a living specification with an executable one. A dated plan then converts an indefinite £14,000 a month into a closed item.

distractors.A: Discovering a regulatory carve-out failure through a mishandled claim means the failure has already happened and is probably reportable. Where the gap is known and cheap to close, shipping the risk to find out is not a decision anyone will defend afterwards.
distractors.B: Paying £14,000 a month to keep two hundred rules alive for the sake of three is disproportionate, and dual-authority creates its own ambiguity about which system's answer governs. If the three rules genuinely need a deterministic check, implement those three as code.
distractors.C: Stuffing two hundred rules into a system prompt does not make behaviour provably equivalent; it makes it long and untested. Equivalence is established by evaluation against cases, not by transcription of the specification into the prompt.

explanation.concept: Decommissioning is blocked by specific unverified behaviours, not by general unease. Enumerate what the legacy system knows that the replacement has not been shown to know, turn each item into a test, put the tests in the regression suite, then retire the legacy system on a date. Undecommissioned predecessors are a standing cost and a standing ambiguity about who is authoritative.
explanation.tip: When a stem quantifies the cost of not sunsetting and names exactly what is unverified, it is asking you to close a small, identified gap with tests — not to accept the cost forever and not to skip the check.

topic: Adoption blocked by unaffordable verification cost
stem: A claims-processing centre deployed a Claude-based first-pass claim summariser. Staff were told headcount will not be cut but that per-handler throughput targets rise from thirty to forty-five claims a day on the day the tool launched. Adoption in week three is 19%. Interviews find handlers do not trust the summaries and are re-reading the full claim file anyway, which makes them slower than before. Which two actions most directly address the cause the interviews revealed? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Publish per-handler adoption leaderboards to the floor so peer comparison drives usage up.
Move the summariser to a higher-capability model tier to raise summary quality before pushing adoption further.
Suspend the throughput target increase until measured handling time with the tool is at or below the pre-tool baseline.
Mandate use of the tool through a policy signed by the operations director and audit compliance weekly.
Make the summariser cite the exact page and paragraph behind every factual assertion, so a handler can verify a point in seconds instead of re-reading the file.

explanation.correct: The interviews identify a verification problem, not a quality problem: handlers cannot cheaply confirm a summary is right, so they redo the work. Citations attack that directly by turning verification from a re-read into a glance, which is the mechanism that makes an assistive summary actually save time. Suspending the throughput increase removes the second cause — a target set on savings that have not been realised, which punishes handlers for the tool's immaturity and guarantees resentment toward it.

distractors.A: Leaderboards raise the cost of not using the tool without lowering the cost of using it. Handlers who distrust the output will click through it to score well, which converts a visible adoption problem into an invisible quality one.
distractors.B: Nothing in the stem says the summaries are wrong; it says handlers cannot tell whether they are right. A better model produces summaries that are equally unverifiable, so the re-reading continues at higher cost per call.
distractors.D: Mandating use has the same defect as the leaderboard and adds a compliance audit. Coercion produces recorded usage, and recorded usage was never the goal. It also attaches the operations director's name to a quality problem nobody has yet fixed.

explanation.concept: Adoption of an AI assistant is governed by the user's cost of verifying its output, not by the output's quality alone. If verifying takes as long as doing the task, the tool cannot save time no matter how good it is. Design for cheap verification — citations, source links, highlighted spans — and do not book the productivity gain in targets before it has been measured.
explanation.tip: When a stem reports what users said in interviews, the key options are the ones that match that stated cause. Coercive and quality-uplift options are perennial distractors because both are things organisations really do when adoption stalls.

topic: Enablement design against reviewer automation bias
stem: At a bank, the trade-surveillance team reviews Claude-generated alert narratives before they are filed. In the pilot, reviewers approved 94% of narratives; a blind audit of the approved set found 8% contained a material factual error. Training to date has covered how to operate the tool. Which additions to the enablement programme address the pattern the audit revealed? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A module on transformer architecture and sampling so reviewers understand the mechanism that produces factual errors in generated narratives.
Calibration sessions on batches containing seeded incorrect narratives, with each reviewer scored on detection and debriefed afterwards.
A quick-reference card of prompt patterns reviewers can use to regenerate any narrative they feel unsure about before approving it.
A minimum four-minute dwell time per narrative, enforced in the tool before the approve control becomes active.
Ongoing blind re-audit of a sample of approved narratives, with results fed back to the individual reviewer who approved them.

explanation.correct: A 94% approval rate against an 8% material error rate is automation bias: reviewers are rubber-stamping fluent output. The counter is practice at discrimination plus a feedback loop. Seeded errors give reviewers repeated, scored exposure to what wrong-but-plausible reads like, which is a skill and not a briefing. Ongoing blind re-audit routed back to the individual keeps the skill from decaying once the pilot glow fades and gives the bank a running measure of review effectiveness rather than review volume.

distractors.A: Knowing why a model can be wrong does not help anyone spot a specific wrong sentence. Mechanism training reliably raises confidence without raising detection, which in a review function is the wrong direction.
distractors.C: Regeneration helps a reviewer who already suspects a problem. The audit shows the failure is upstream of suspicion — reviewers are not detecting errors, so they never reach the point of regenerating.
distractors.D: Dwell time measures presence, not attention, and is trivially satisfied by leaving the tab open. Enforcing time-on-task without teaching what to look for produces slower rubber-stamping. Reviewers under quota pressure will leave the tab open and work on something else.

explanation.concept: Where a human sits in the loop to catch AI errors, that human's detection rate is itself a system parameter and must be trained and measured. Use seeded errors to calibrate and blind re-audit to monitor. A review step whose effectiveness is never measured is a control on the diagram, not a control in the system.
explanation.tip: High approval rate plus a non-trivial audited error rate is the exam's standard signature for automation bias. The answers are always calibration and measurement, never mechanism education or enforced slowness.

topic: Matching post-launch review cadence to change frequency
stem: A media company launched a Claude-based subtitle-localisation QA assistant. Leadership has proposed a quarterly steering review as the only post-launch checkpoint. The team ships prompt changes weekly and the content mix shifts seasonally. During the pilot, quality dipped and the team could not tell which of the eleven prompt changes made since the previous look had caused it. What review cadence should the architect argue for?

options.text: Quarterly steering only, backed by automated alerting on quality thresholds so that humans get involved exactly when a threshold is breached rather than on a fixed schedule that may find nothing.
A single monthly review at all levels, replacing both the weekly operational rhythm and the quarterly steering meeting with one consistent cadence.
A weekly operational review of quality metrics and sampled failures owned by the delivery team, with the quarterly steering review retained for scope and budget.
A review triggered by each prompt change rather than at fixed intervals, so every change is examined at the moment it ships.

explanation.correct: The pilot already demonstrated the cost of a review interval longer than the change interval: eleven changes accumulated between looks and the regression could not be attributed to any of them. Reviewing at least as often as you change restores attribution. The two cadences serve different questions — weekly answers "is quality holding and what changed", quarterly answers "is this still worth the investment and what should it do next" — and collapsing them loses one of the two.

distractors.A: Threshold alerting catches sharp breaks and misses slow drift, seasonal mix shifts, and the class of failure nobody thought to write a threshold for. It also gives no forum for reading sampled failures, which is where new failure modes are discovered.
distractors.B: Monthly still lets roughly four prompt changes accumulate between looks, so the attribution problem persists in milder form. It also drags executives into operational detail while starving the team of a fast feedback loop.
distractors.D: Per-change review sounds rigorous but is the job of the pre-merge evaluation gate, not of a review meeting. It also gives no periodic view of drift and seasonal effects, which appear between changes rather than because of them.

explanation.concept: Set the operational review interval no longer than the interval at which the system changes, so a quality movement can be attributed to a specific change. Keep the strategic cadence separate and slower: it answers investment and direction questions that weekly data cannot inform.
explanation.tip: The decisive sentence is the one about eleven changes since the last look. When a stem tells you attribution already failed once, the answer is the cadence that restores it, not the one with the best-sounding governance.

topic: Prioritising an improvement backlog by quantified loss
stem: Three months after launch, a travel company's Claude-based itinerary-change assistant has a crowded improvement backlog. Production data: hallucinated fare rules appear in 0.6% of the 40,000 conversations a month, and each one that reaches a customer costs £180 on average in goodwill refunds; tone is criticised in 22% of CSAT free-text comments; p95 latency is 4.1 seconds against a 3-second internal target; and a requested Portuguese expansion would open a market worth £2m a year in bookings at a 4% margin. Which should be prioritised first?

options.text: Bring p95 latency under the three-second target, since it is the only stated service objective currently in breach and breaches tend to compound as volume grows.
Ship the Portuguese expansion while the market opportunity is uncontested, deferring quality work to the following quarter when the revenue can fund it.
Address the tone complaints, which affect the largest share of customers who took the trouble to comment and shape the brand impression the assistant creates.
Cut the fare-rule hallucination rate, and gate other changes behind a groundedness evaluation until it comes down.

explanation.correct: Work the numbers. 0.6% of 40,000 conversations is 240 a month, at £180 each that is £43,200 a month or roughly £518,000 a year of direct loss. The Portuguese market is worth £2m in bookings at 4% margin, which is £80,000 a year, and that is upside rather than realised loss. Latency and tone are real but carry no quantified financial figure in the stem. The hallucination line is more than six times the next largest number and is also the only item that damages trust in the assistant's core function.

distractors.A: A 1.1-second overshoot on an internal target is a genuine defect and worth a place in the backlog, but the stem attaches no cost to it. Prioritising a self-imposed threshold over a half-million-pound annual loss inverts the ranking.
distractors.B: Expanding a system that produces incorrect fare rules multiplies the defect across a new market and a new language, where the groundedness evaluation does not yet exist. The margin figure is also the smaller number once you compute it.
distractors.C: Twenty-two percent is the largest-looking percentage in the stem, which is precisely why it is the trap: it is a share of the self-selected subset of customers who left a comment, and it is attached to no financial consequence.

explanation.concept: Prioritise a post-launch backlog on expected value, not on the size of the raw percentages or the loudness of the request. Convert every candidate to the same unit — money per period, or incidents per period weighted by severity — before comparing. Percentages with different denominators are not comparable, and upside is not the same currency as realised loss.
explanation.tip: When a stem hands you four items each with different units, it is a computation question wearing a prioritisation costume. Do the multiplications before you read the options; the biggest percentage is almost never the biggest number.

topic: Evidence that ownership transfer to a run team is complete
stem: A build team is transferring a production Claude system to a separate run team. Which condition most reliably indicates the transfer is genuinely complete?

options.text: The run team has independently executed a rollback and a pinned-model-version change in production, unaided, with the build team absent.
The run team has attended an architecture walkthrough and received the full handover documentation pack.
The build team has closed every open defect on the backlog and the change freeze has been lifted.
Dashboards and alert routing have been repointed to the run team's on-call rota and paging schedule.

explanation.correct: Ownership is a demonstrated capability, not a set of delivered artefacts. The two operations that define control of an AI system in production are reverting a change and moving a pinned version, and a run team that has performed both without help can act in the incident that matters. Rehearsing the transfer this way also surfaces the gaps the documentation glossed over — missing credentials, an approval nobody can grant out of hours, a command that only works from a build-team laptop — while the original team is still available to fix them.

distractors.B: Walkthroughs and document packs are inputs to transfer, not evidence of it. Every failed handover in history included a well-attended walkthrough; the gap shows up the first time the receiving team has to act alone.
distractors.C: A zero-defect backlog is neither achievable nor relevant. Run teams inherit open defects routinely; what they cannot inherit is an inability to operate the system. Handovers routinely and correctly complete with a backlog attached and an agreed plan for it.
distractors.D: Repointing alerts is necessary and easy, and is often mistaken for the whole job. It routes the page to a team that may still have no rehearsed way to respond to it.

explanation.concept: Close a handover on demonstrated competence: the receiving team performs the critical operations in the real environment, unaided, before the building team disengages. Define the short list of operations that constitute control of the system — rollback, version change, guardrail toggle, escalation — and require each to be exercised.
explanation.tip: In handover items, prefer the option where the receiving team does something over the option where they are given something. Documentation, dashboards and walkthroughs are all real work, but none of them prove capability.

topic: Purpose of a parallel run during system replacement
stem: When an AI system is replacing an incumbent production system, what is the purpose of a parallel run?

options.text: To split load across both systems during transition so neither has to be provisioned for full production capacity.
To record where the two systems disagree on live traffic while the incumbent stays authoritative.
To let each user choose which system to work in, making adoption voluntary and reducing resistance to the change.
To satisfy a control requiring that two independent systems approve every transaction on an ongoing basis.

explanation.correct: A parallel run feeds real production traffic to the replacement while every consequential decision still belongs to the incumbent. The output is a disagreement log: a small, information-dense set of cases where the two systems differ, which humans adjudicate to establish whether the replacement is better, worse, or differently wrong. Errors are therefore discovered on real inputs before any of them can cause harm, which is what makes this the standard de-risking step when the errors in question are expensive.

distractors.A: That describes load sharing between two live systems. In a parallel run both systems process the same traffic rather than a share of it, so it increases total cost rather than reducing capacity needs.
distractors.C: User choice between two systems is an opt-in rollout, a different technique with a different purpose. It also produces self-selected populations, which contaminates any comparison you might want to draw.
distractors.D: Permanent dual approval is a segregation-of-duties control, not a migration technique. A parallel run is explicitly temporary and ends at cutover. It also describes a permanent arrangement, whereas a parallel run is scoped and ends on a date the migration plan sets.

explanation.concept: Parallel running is how you de-risk replacing a system whose errors are expensive: same inputs, both systems, incumbent authoritative, disagreements adjudicated. Budget for the adjudication effort, agree in advance what disagreement profile permits cutover, and set an end date so the parallel state does not become permanent.
explanation.tip: Distinguish parallel run from load sharing and from opt-in rollout. The defining features are identical traffic to both systems and only one of them being allowed to act.

topic: Pilot design when the target failure mode is rare
stem: A pharmacy chain is designing a pilot for a Claude-based prescription-interaction checker. Two designs cost the same: six pharmacies for twelve weeks, or sixty pharmacies for two weeks. Each pharmacy dispenses roughly 400 scripts a week. The failure the safety board cares about is a missed interaction involving a drug that appears in fewer than one in five thousand scripts. Which design should the architect recommend?

options.text: Six pharmacies for twelve weeks, because a longer exposure lets pharmacists' override behaviour stabilise past the novelty period and gives a truer picture of steady-state use.
Sixty pharmacies for two weeks, because it puts roughly 48,000 scripts through the checker against 28,800 for the alternative, so more of the rare interactions actually occur.

Either duration, provided the rare-interaction failure is tested offline on a constructed set of known interaction cases and the pilot is used for what only live use reveals: workflow fit and override behaviour.
Neither yet; postpone the pilot until offline agreement with the chain's existing interaction database exceeds 99.9%, since safety work should not begin in live pharmacies at all.

explanation.correct: Both designs are hopeless for the stated failure. At one in five thousand, 48,000 scripts yield around nine or ten instances and 28,800 yield around six — far too few to estimate a miss rate for a safety board, and that is before allowing for whether a miss is even noticed. Rare failure modes are characterised by constructing cases, not by waiting for them, and a constructed set can contain hundreds of known interactions at no risk. The pilot is then spent on the questions no offline set can answer: does it fit the counter workflow, and do pharmacists override it appropriately.

distractors.A: The steady-state argument is sound on its own terms and is a real reason to prefer longer pilots. It does not rescue the design, because twelve weeks in six pharmacies sees even fewer rare interactions than the wide alternative.
distractors.B: The arithmetic is right and the conclusion still fails: ten expected events cannot support a rate estimate precise enough to clear a safety board, and two weeks is too short to observe how pharmacists settle into using the tool.
distractors.D: Agreement with the existing database measures reproduction of the incumbent, not safety, and a 99.9% bar on a system that will disagree for good reasons is unreachable. It also indefinitely postpones learning anything about live workflow fit.

explanation.concept: Choose the measurement instrument that matches the event rate. Rare, high-severity failures are established with constructed evaluation sets built from known cases; live pilots measure things that only appear in real use — workflow fit, override behaviour, handoff friction. Sizing a pilot to catch a one-in-thousands event is almost always infeasible, and pretending otherwise buys false assurance.
explanation.tip: When a stem gives you an event rate and asks you to size an exposure, multiply it out. If the expected count comes back in single or low double digits, the intended answer is that the pilot is the wrong instrument for that question.

topic: Go/no-go when a pre-agreed criterion is not yet measurable
stem: A B2B SaaS company finished a four-week pilot of a Claude-based onboarding-email drafter. The criterion agreed before the pilot was: median time to send a first onboarding email drops from 22 minutes to under 10, with no increase in the 30-day churn rate of accounts onboarded during the pilot. Median time came in at 8 minutes. The churn figure cannot exist for another 30 days because the pilot cohort has only just onboarded. The sponsor wants a go/no-go today. What is the next step?

options.text: Declare a no-go, because a criterion that cannot be evaluated at the decision point must be treated as unmet.
Declare a go on the strength of the time result, since churn is a lagging indicator that would not have been available in time for any four-week pilot's decision.
Agree a leading proxy for churn, such as seven-day activation rate on the pilot cohort, and read the go/no-go against that proxy instead.
Hold the decision for 30 days with the pilot cohort still running, and tell the sponsor the churn half of the criterion is why the decision waits.

explanation.correct: The criterion was written with two halves for a reason: faster emails that lose accounts are not a win, and the sponsor agreed to that framing before any data existed. Rolling out now does not make the churn number arrive sooner, so the only thing waiting costs is thirty days of unrealised benefit on a cohort that is already onboarded. Keeping the pilot running preserves the measurement and lets the conversation with the sponsor be about the criterion they signed, not about the pressure of the meeting.

distractors.A: Not-yet-measured is not the same as failed. Treating an unread criterion as a failure discards a pilot that met half its bar and is thirty days from a complete answer, and it teaches teams to write criteria they can read quickly rather than criteria that matter.
distractors.B: The lagging-indicator argument is genuinely true and is exactly why churn should be scrutinised when the criterion is drafted. Once it is in the agreed criterion, dropping it at readout because it is inconvenient is how a pilot with criteria degrades into a pilot without them.
distractors.C: Choosing a proxy after seeing the favourable half of the result is criterion-shopping, even when the proxy is defensible. Seven-day activation agreed before the pilot would have been fine; agreed now, it is a substitution made under pressure to produce a yes.

explanation.concept: Criteria are binding in both directions. Once a threshold is agreed before the pilot, you neither waive it because it is slow to read nor swap it for a proxy after seeing partial results. If a criterion's measurement window exceeds the pilot window, resolve that at design time — shorten the criterion, lengthen the pilot, or pre-agree the proxy.
explanation.tip: Watch the sequencing. An option that would have been the right answer if it appeared at pilot design time is often the wrong answer when it appears at readout, because by then the data has been seen.
